note: Curated waypoint descriptions, keyed by the stable ids in data/waypoint-ids.json. Applied by scripts/build-trails.ts (overriding any description from the GPX/GeoJSON source) and uploadable to the comments API with scripts/upload-descriptions.ts. The main-line entries come first, listed south to north from Walhalla to Tharwa in the km order of the generated trail data; the off-trail, alternate-route and side-trip entries follow, ordered by their position along the same line. An entry is keyed by waypoint id, so one entry covers every list a waypoint appears in.

descriptions.name: O'Sheas Mill Site
descriptions.description: Old timber mill site in the Tyers valley, now a flat clearing used as the first camp out of Walhalla. Water comes from the river beside it rather than a tank, so treat what you collect.

descriptions.name: Tyers River East
descriptions.description: The east branch of the Tyers River at the O'Sheas Mill Site clearing. Bigger than the creeks up on the ridge, but still river water in forest country — treat it before drinking.

descriptions.name: Mountain Monarchs
descriptions.description: Camp among tall wet forest on the long climb from the Tyers valley towards the Baw Baw plateau. No water is marked at the site, so fill down at the river before you start up.

descriptions.name: Mushroom Rocks
descriptions.description: Camp beside the weathered granite tors of Mushroom Rocks, a well-known landmark on the climb onto the Baw Baw plateau. Exposed to wind, and no water is marked here.

descriptions.name: Talbot Hut Site
descriptions.description: Clearing on the Baw Baw plateau where Talbot Hut once stood; only the site remains. Snow gums and open plateau country, with no water marked at the site itself.

descriptions.name: Rock Shelter
descriptions.description: Rock overhang on the Baw Baw plateau, used as a rough camp and as somewhere to sit out weather. Cramped rather than comfortable, and no water is marked here.

descriptions.name: Rock Shelter
descriptions.description: A second rock-shelter pitch a little further along the plateau. Like its neighbour it suits a night out of the wind more than a planned camp, and has no marked water.

descriptions.name: Whitelaw Hut Site
descriptions.description: Site of the former Whitelaw Hut in the snow gums near Mt Whitelaw. The hut is long gone; the clearing is still used as a camp, and no water is marked at it.

descriptions.name: Near Mt Whitelaw
descriptions.description: Open camp in the snow gums close to Mt Whitelaw, near the northern end of the Baw Baw plateau before the long descent towards the Thomson. No marked water here.

descriptions.name: Stronarchs Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp on the ridge falling away from the Baw Baw plateau towards the Thomson River. It sits high above the river, so carry water up for the night.

descriptions.name: Thomson River
descriptions.description: The Thomson River at the foot of the long descent off the Baw Baw plateau, and the largest water on this stretch. Treat it, and take on what you need before the climb out.

descriptions.name: Thomson River
descriptions.description: Another access point to the Thomson as the track works along the valley. A good place to drink and refill, after treating.

descriptions.name: Thomson River Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp on the flats beside the Thomson River, the low point between the Baw Baw plateau and the climb north. Shaded, with river water alongside that needs treating.

descriptions.name: Thomson River
descriptions.description: River access at the Thomson River camping area. Fill properly here — the climb north is long and the ridges above carry little water.

descriptions.name: Jordan River
descriptions.description: The Jordan River in the low country between the Thomson and the ranges to the north. A river rather than a trickle, but still treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Blue Jacket Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp near the Jordan River at Blue Jacket, in old goldfields country. River water is close by; treat it, and expect a warm, low-altitude night compared with the plateau behind.

descriptions.name: Jordan River
descriptions.description: The last marked access to the Jordan River before the long climb north. Load up here, and treat what you carry.

descriptions.name: bobs hut
descriptions.description: The water source at Bob's Hut. Like most creeks at this height it runs with the season, so check it rather than assume it, and treat what you collect.

descriptions.name: Bob's Hut
descriptions.description: Small timber hut in the ranges north of the Jordan River, one of the old high-country huts kept as a shelter rather than as accommodation. Camp outside if others are using it and leave it as you found it.

descriptions.name: Fiddlers Green
descriptions.description: Grassy clearing a little over a kilometre on from Bob's Hut, and a popular camp on this section. The hut's creek is the marked water, and it can be low late in summer.

descriptions.name: Black River
descriptions.description: The Black River, down in the valley between the ranges. Larger than the ridge creeks either side, though still to be treated — and there is a stiff climb out whichever way you are heading.

descriptions.name: Middle Ridge Rd 1
descriptions.description: Creek crossing on Middle Ridge Road, up in the snow gums. Good after rain and unreliable in a dry late summer, so look before you plan on it, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Middle Ridge Rd 2
descriptions.description: A second creek on Middle Ridge Road. If the first crossing was dry expect the same here, and plan the section on what you are carrying rather than on what is marked.

descriptions.name: Rumpff Saddle
descriptions.description: Saddle where several high-country tracks meet, long used as a camp on the AAWT. Open, exposed, and with no water marked at the saddle itself.

descriptions.name: Middle Ridge Rd
descriptions.description: Roadside camp on Middle Ridge Road in the snow gums. Flat ground with vehicle access; the nearest marked water is at the creek crossings back down the road.

descriptions.name: Low Saddle
descriptions.description: Camp at Low Saddle, a dip in the ridge on the long traverse towards the Howitt country. No water at the saddle — the nearest marked source is a couple of kilometres further on.

descriptions.name: Low Saddle Rd
descriptions.description: Creek on Low Saddle Road, the nearest marked water to the Low Saddle camp. A small mountain creek: fine after rain, easily dry in a hot spell, and worth treating.

descriptions.name: Nobs Track
descriptions.description: Creek crossing on Nobs Track, high in the snow gums. Small and seasonal — carry enough to reach it comfortably, and treat whatever you find.

descriptions.name: Chesters Yard
descriptions.description: Old stockmen's yard site on the high country south of Mt Howitt, now a well-used camp with vehicle access. Exposed when the weather turns, and no water is marked at the yard.

descriptions.name: Brocks Rd
descriptions.description: Camp beside Brocks Road in the snow gums at around 1,600 m, one of the higher roadside sites on the trail. Cold and open to the wind, with no marked water.

descriptions.name: Hellfire Creek
descriptions.description: Hellfire Creek, a small alpine stream in the Howitt country. Snowmelt keeps it going into early summer and it fades later in the season, so treat what you collect.

descriptions.name: Hellfire Creek Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp beside Hellfire Creek, one of the last sheltered sites before the high open ground around Mt Howitt. Check the creek is running before you plan the night around it, and treat the water.

descriptions.name: Howitt Creek
descriptions.description: Alpine creek on the approach to Mt Howitt, high in the snow gums. It runs hard with snowmelt and weakens through summer, so treat what you take and have a fallback if it is dry.

descriptions.name: Near Mt Speculation
descriptions.description: Camp in the snow gums near Mt Speculation, on the rugged section beyond the Crosscut Saw. A popular stop and a spectacular one, but very exposed in bad weather.

descriptions.name: Camp Creek
descriptions.description: Camp Creek, the marked water for the Mt Speculation camping area. Seasonal like everything at this height — treat it, and expect little more than a trickle late in summer.

descriptions.name: Catherine Saddle
descriptions.description: Saddle camp between Mt Speculation and the Viking country, lower and more sheltered than the peaks either side. No water is marked at the saddle.

descriptions.name: Speculation Rd
descriptions.description: Creek on Speculation Road, the nearest marked water to Catherine Saddle. Small and seasonal — check it rather than count on it in late summer, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Viking Saddle
descriptions.description: Camp in the saddle below The Viking, at the foot of one of the steepest and most exposed climbs on the whole trail. No water is marked here, so arrive carrying enough.

descriptions.name: Viking Saddle
descriptions.description: A second marked pitch in Viking Saddle. Like its neighbour it has no water, so fill before you drop into the saddle for the night.

descriptions.name: Barry Saddle
descriptions.description: Rainwater tank at Barry Saddle, one of the tanks that make the dry Barry Mountains section workable. Tank levels depend on recent rain and on other walkers, so treat the water and never assume it is full.

descriptions.name: Barry Saddle Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp at Barry Saddle beside the tank, a natural break after the Viking. Carry a reserve in case the tank is low when you get there.

descriptions.name: Selwyn Track
descriptions.description: Roadside camp on the Selwyn Track in the Barry Mountains — dry ridge country where the marked water is tanks rather than creeks. Plan the day around the tanks.

descriptions.name: East Riley Rd
descriptions.description: Rainwater tank on East Riley Road in the Barry Mountains. Check it as soon as you arrive, because a tank in this dry ridge country can be empty, and treat what you draw.

descriptions.name: South Selwyn
descriptions.description: Tank on the South Selwyn section of the Barry Mountains, high on the ridge with no creek at hand. Treat the water and fill right up — the next marked source is several hours on.

descriptions.name: Selwyn Creek Road
descriptions.description: Camp on Selwyn Creek Road towards the northern end of the Barry Mountains. The creek that gives the road its name is the nearest marked water.

descriptions.name: Mt Selwyn Creek
descriptions.description: Creek below Mt Selwyn, the first natural water after a long stretch of tank-fed ridge walking. Treat it, and don't assume it is running in a dry late summer.

descriptions.name: Murrays Hut Site
descriptions.description: Clearing where Murrays Hut once stood, on the high ground of the Barry Mountains. The hut is gone; the site is still used as a camp and has no marked water.

descriptions.name: The Twins
descriptions.description: Rainwater tank at The Twins, high on the ridge with no creek nearby. Check the level before you commit to camping here, and treat whatever you take.

descriptions.name: Twins Track 1
descriptions.description: Camp on the Twins Track, high under snow gums near The Twins. A tank stands close by, but arrive ready to be self-sufficient for water.

descriptions.name: Twins Track 2
descriptions.description: A second camp along the Twins Track, a little lower and often better sheltered than the first. Water means the tank behind you or the creek ahead.

descriptions.name: Twins Track
descriptions.description: Creek crossing high on the Twins Track. At this altitude the flow is driven by snowmelt and does not last, so treat it and have a plan if the bed is dry.

descriptions.name: Blowhard Hut
descriptions.description: Small hut on Blowhard Spur, on the approach to Mt Hotham. A shelter for a break or an emergency rather than a bookable bed; camp outside if it is occupied.

descriptions.name: Diamantina Hut
descriptions.description: Historic shelter hut on the high ground at Mt Hotham, close to the Great Alpine Road. Road access and the Hotham village nearby make this the obvious resupply or exit point on this half of the trail, though what is open varies with the season.

descriptions.name: Derrick Hut
descriptions.description: Small alpine hut on the high ground north of Hotham, built as a refuge for skiers and walkers caught out by weather. Keep it clear for emergencies and camp outside in good conditions.

descriptions.name: Dibbins Hut
descriptions.description: Historic cattlemen's hut on the Cobungra River flats below Mt Loch, one of the classic stops on the crossing between Hotham and the Bogong High Plains. River water at hand, and it needs treating.

descriptions.name: Dibbins Hut
descriptions.description: A second marker for the Dibbins Hut site on the Cobungra flats. Grassy camping around the hut with the river alongside; treat the water before drinking.

descriptions.name: Cope Saddle Hut
descriptions.description: Small shelter hut at Cope Saddle on the Bogong High Plains, in open alpine country with next to nothing between you and the wind. A refuge rather than a place to plan a night in.

descriptions.name: Pretty Valley Ck Trib
descriptions.description: Small tributary in the Pretty Valley on the Bogong High Plains, fed by snowmelt and the bogs above. The flow falls away through summer, so treat what you collect and check it before relying on it.

descriptions.name: Cope Hut
descriptions.description: One of the best-known huts on the Bogong High Plains, built in the early days of alpine skiing and long used as a base by skiers and walkers. There is camping around it, and any water nearby is alpine seepage — treat it.

descriptions.name: Wallaces Hut
descriptions.description: The oldest surviving cattlemen's hut on the Bogong High Plains, built by the Wallace brothers in the 1880s and now a heritage site. Day visitors are common; camp in the snow gums nearby rather than in the hut.

descriptions.name: Langford West Aqueduct 2
descriptions.description: Water at the Langford West aqueduct, part of the old channel system that moves high-plains water for the hydro scheme. There can be water here when the surface creeks are thin, but check it rather than count on it, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Langford Gap Hut
descriptions.description: Shelter hut at Langford Gap, out on the open Bogong High Plains with vehicle tracks close by. Very useful in weather; the surrounding plain offers no shelter at all.

descriptions.name: Langford Gap
descriptions.description: Marked water at Langford Gap, where the high plains road crosses this open country. Alpine water here is seasonal and often shallow — treat it and carry a reserve.

descriptions.name: Langford East Aqueduct
descriptions.description: The eastern arm of the Langford aqueduct on the high plains. Like the western channel it can be low or stagnant depending on the season, so look before you plan on it and treat anything you take.

descriptions.name: Edmonson Hut
descriptions.description: High shelter hut in open alpine country on the Bogong High Plains, at more than 1,800 m. There is little natural shelter around it, which is exactly why it is there.

descriptions.name: Duane Creek
descriptions.description: The creek at Ropers Hut, at the top of Duane Spur. It is the last marked water before the long descent to Big River, and like everything up here it is seasonal — treat it.

descriptions.name: Ropers Hut
descriptions.description: Hut on the northern edge of the Bogong High Plains, at the head of the long descent to Big River, and rebuilt after fire went through this country. A creek runs nearby; treat the water and fill before the drop.

descriptions.name: Big River 1
descriptions.description: A second marked pitch on the Big River flats. Whichever you use, take on water and food here — the climb out is long and steep in either direction.

descriptions.name: Big River
descriptions.description: Big River at the bottom of the Duane Spur descent, a genuine river and the low point between the Bogong High Plains and Mt Wills. Crossings can be deep and pushy after rain or heavy snowmelt; treat the water.

descriptions.name: Big River 2
descriptions.description: Camping on the Big River flats, the traditional break between the descent off the high plains and the climb up T Spur. Low, shaded ground with the river alongside.

descriptions.name: T Spur
descriptions.description: Marked water well up the T Spur climb out of Big River. It is a small alpine source that can fail late in the season, so start the climb carrying enough rather than banking on it.

descriptions.name: Big River Rd
descriptions.description: Creek on Big River Road on the approach to Mt Wills. Small and seasonal like the rest of the ridge water; check it is flowing before you plan the night around it, and treat it.

descriptions.name: Mt Wills Hut
descriptions.description: Hut high on Mt Wills among the snow gums and alpine ash, a classic overnight stop on this section. No water is marked up on the ridge, so carry what you need for the night.

descriptions.name: Gill Creek
descriptions.description: Creek well down the long descent from Mt Wills towards the Mitta Mitta. Lower and better sheltered than the ridge creeks, but still seasonal — treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Four Mile Ck
descriptions.description: Small creek in the low country above the Mitta Mitta valley. Worth a look rather than a plan in a dry spell, and treat anything you collect.

descriptions.name: Taylors Crossing Campsite
descriptions.description: Camping area at Taylors Crossing on the Mitta Mitta River, one of the lowest points on the trail and a common road-access and food-drop spot. Hot in summer, with river water alongside.

descriptions.name: Mitta Mitta River
descriptions.description: The Mitta Mitta at Taylors Crossing. It drains a large mountain catchment and carries water when the high creeks have stopped, but it is river water — treat it before drinking.

descriptions.name: Kennedys Hut
descriptions.description: Old hut in the Mitta Mitta valley near Taylors Crossing, down in dry, low country a long way below the alps either side. The river close by is the water; treat it.

descriptions.name: Morass Ck (Treat - Farmland)
descriptions.description: Morass Creek, running through farmland as the name on the waypoint warns. Stock and paddock runoff make treatment essential rather than optional here, and the flow varies with the season.

descriptions.name: Johnies Top
descriptions.description: Rainwater tank high on Johnies Top, on the long dry climb towards the Cobberas. There is no creek up here, so check the tank as soon as you reach it and treat what you draw.

descriptions.name: Corner Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the valley country on the way towards Buenba. A modest mountain stream: good after rain, thin in a dry late summer, and worth treating.

descriptions.name: Buenba Flat South #1
descriptions.description: Camp on the open grassy flats at Buenba, soft, sheltered ground after the ridges either side. Creek water alongside, and flats like this hold cold air overnight.

descriptions.name: Buenba Creek
descriptions.description: Buenba Creek on the flats of the same name, the marked water for the camping here. Grazing country in places upstream, so treat it, and expect less of it as summer wears on.

descriptions.name: Buckwong Track
descriptions.description: Creek crossing on the Buckwong Track in the Cobberas country. Small, seasonal and best treated; the creek at the hut ahead is the other option nearby.

descriptions.name: Buckwong Hut
descriptions.description: Hut on Buckwong Creek in the Cobberas foothills, a welcome bit of shelter in a remote stretch. The creek close by is the water and needs treating.

descriptions.name: Buckwong Creek
descriptions.description: Buckwong Creek at the hut, the marked water for this section. Rain and snowmelt drive it, so it can be low late in the season — treat what you collect.

descriptions.name: Buckwong Hut
descriptions.description: A second marker for the Buckwong Hut site. Flat ground for tents around the hut, with the creek alongside for water.

descriptions.name: Dead Horse Ck
descriptions.description: Dead Horse Creek, in the remote country south of Limestone Creek. A small stream that runs with the season, so treat it and don't build the day around it in a dry spell.

descriptions.name: Limestone Creek
descriptions.description: Limestone Creek, in a valley with vehicle access and a well-used camping area. Larger than most creeks on this section though still seasonal, and it should be treated.

descriptions.name: Claire Creek
descriptions.description: Small creek near Limestone Creek. Useful as a top-up rather than a destination; check it rather than assume it, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Cowombat Flat Tk 1
descriptions.description: Creek on the Cowombat Flat Track, up in the Cobberas. High, small and seasonal — treat it, and carry enough that finding it dry is not a problem.

descriptions.name: Bulley Creek
descriptions.description: Bulley Creek on the approach to Cowombat Flat. A headwater stream, so the flow is modest at best and can disappear altogether in a dry summer.

descriptions.name: Cowombat Flat Tk 2
descriptions.description: A second creek on the Cowombat Flat Track. If the first was dry expect the same here, and treat whatever you do find.

descriptions.name: Cowombat Flat
descriptions.description: Big grassy flat at the head of the Murray on the Victoria–New South Wales border, with the wreck of a crashed RAAF Dakota nearby. A classic AAWT camp, open and cold at night.

descriptions.name: Murray River
descriptions.description: The Murray River at Cowombat Flat, barely more than a stream this close to its source. Treat what you take, and expect headwater flow rather than a river.

descriptions.name: Pilot Creek
descriptions.description: Creek below The Pilot with good camping on the grassy ground beside it. Headwater country, so the flow is seasonal — check it before relying on it and treat what you collect.

descriptions.name: Tin Mine Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the old Tin Mine country of southern Kosciuszko National Park. A small mountain stream that varies a lot with the season; treat what you collect.

descriptions.name: Ingeegoodbee River
descriptions.description: The Ingeegoodbee River at the Tin Mine Huts, the marked water for this camp. A small upland river: check the level rather than assume it, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Tin Mine Huts
descriptions.description: Historic huts at the old Tin Mine workings in southern Kosciuszko, remnants of the district's mining and grazing past. A landmark stop — camp outside and leave the huts as you find them.

descriptions.name: Cascade Trail
descriptions.description: Creek on the Cascade Trail in southern Kosciuszko. Snowmelt-fed and seasonal like the rest of the water up here; treat what you collect.

descriptions.name: Cascade Hut
descriptions.description: Historic grazing hut on the Cascade Trail, one of the best-kept old huts in the park and a popular day-walk destination. Open grassy surrounds for camping; leave the hut clear for shelter.

descriptions.name: Cascade Creek 1
descriptions.description: Cascade Creek at the hut. A clear alpine stream, and like all of them it should be checked rather than assumed and treated before drinking.

descriptions.name: Cascade Creek 2
descriptions.description: A second crossing of Cascade Creek along the trail. Same water and the same caution: treat it, and take what you need before the climb ahead.

descriptions.name: Thredbo River 1
descriptions.description: The upper Thredbo River, high in its catchment. A river rather than a creek, though still snow-fed and thinner late in summer — treat it.

descriptions.name: Thredbo River 2
descriptions.description: A second access to the upper Thredbo. Worth filling properly: the climb onto the Main Range is long and there is no shelter once you are up there.

descriptions.name: Snowy River 1
descriptions.description: The infant Snowy River, high on the Main Range at around 2,040 m and the highest marked water on the trail. Snowmelt drives it, so it is at its strongest in spring; treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Anton Anderson Saddle
descriptions.description: Camp in a saddle high on the Main Range, well above the treeline. Superb country and completely exposed — pitch low, peg well, and check the park's current alpine camping restrictions before choosing a spot.

descriptions.name: Pounds Creek Trib
descriptions.description: Small tributary of Pounds Creek high on the Main Range, fed by snowmelt and alpine bog. It runs best early in the season; treat what you collect.

descriptions.name: Consett Stephen Pass
descriptions.description: High pass camp on the northern Main Range, at around 1,910 m. Magnificent and entirely open to the weather; check current alpine camping restrictions before pitching.

descriptions.name: Whites River Hut
descriptions.description: Shelter hut near the Munyang River in the Snowy Mountains, one of the huts kept for emergency use in this exposed country. Camp outside; the river is close by for water.

descriptions.name: Munyang River
descriptions.description: The Munyang River at Whites River Hut. An upland river fed by the range above — treat it, and note that flows drop away through summer.

descriptions.name: Dickie Cooper Creek 1
descriptions.description: Creek on the high ground near Schlink Pass. Bog- and snowmelt-fed, small, and seasonal; treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Dickie Cooper Creek 2
descriptions.description: A second crossing of Dickie Cooper Creek. Handy for a quick top-up near Schlink Hut, after treating.

descriptions.name: Schlink Hut
descriptions.description: Substantial hut at Schlink Pass, dating from the Snowy Mountains scheme era and now a well-known walkers' shelter. High and exposed, with creek water close by.

descriptions.name: Dickie Cooper Creek 3
descriptions.description: The last marked crossing of Dickie Cooper Creek north of Schlink Pass. Treat it, and fill before the open country ahead.

descriptions.name: Valentines Hut
descriptions.description: Small hut in the Valentine country north of Schlink Pass, in open snow-grass surrounds. A shelter rather than accommodation — camp outside and keep it clear.

descriptions.name: Back Flat Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the broad snow-grass flats south of Jagungal. Bog-fed water that is often tannin-stained and slow-moving; treat it.

descriptions.name: Grey Mare Hut
descriptions.description: Marked water at Grey Mare Hut, in the old mining country west of Jagungal. Alpine creek water — check that it is running and treat it before drinking.

descriptions.name: Tooma River
descriptions.description: The Tooma River in its headwaters below Jagungal. A river by name and a small one at this altitude, so treat it and don't count on a strong flow late in summer.

descriptions.name: Tumut River
descriptions.description: The upper Tumut in the Jagungal country. Snow-fed headwaters: fuller early in the season, thinner later, and always worth treating.

descriptions.name: Tumut River Trib
descriptions.description: Small tributary of the upper Tumut on the way past Jagungal. Seasonal and easily reduced to a damp line in dry years; treat what you take.

descriptions.name: O' Keefes Hut
descriptions.description: Hut in the open country near Mt Jagungal and a familiar landmark in the Jagungal Wilderness. Creek water nearby; camp outside and leave the hut for shelter.

descriptions.name: Hut Creek
descriptions.description: The creek beside O'Keefes Hut. Like most water in the Jagungal Wilderness it comes from bog and snowmelt, so check it rather than assume it, and treat it.

descriptions.name: Bogong Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the snow-grass country north of Jagungal. Small and seasonal — a top-up rather than a source to build a day around, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Doubtful Creek
descriptions.description: Doubtful Creek, a name worth taking at face value in late summer. Treat what you collect and carry enough that a dry bed does not matter.

descriptions.name: Diggers Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the old grazing country north of Jagungal. A modest flow that falls away through summer; treat it before drinking.

descriptions.name: Mackays Hut
descriptions.description: Hut in the Jagungal Wilderness, one of the chain of grazing-era shelters through this country. The creek nearby is the water; camp outside and leave the hut clear.

descriptions.name: Tibeaudo Creek
descriptions.description: The creek at Mackays Hut. Bog-fed alpine water: treat it, and expect it to be slow or low in a dry season.

descriptions.name: McKeahnies Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the rolling country between Jagungal and the Tantangara plains. Seasonal, so check it before planning a camp around it, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Barneys Creek
descriptions.description: Small creek in the same open country. Fine as a top-up once treated, but not a source to count on in late summer.

descriptions.name: Nine Mile Creek
descriptions.description: Creek high on the long, thinly watered stretch towards the Eucumbene. Small and seasonal — check it, treat it, and carry a reserve either way.

descriptions.name: Eucumbene River
descriptions.description: The Eucumbene River in its upper valley, one of the larger crossings on this section. Treat it, and take on water before the climb out.

descriptions.name: Chance Creek
descriptions.description: Creek between the Eucumbene and the Tantangara country. As the name suggests, worth a look rather than a certainty — and treat anything you find.

descriptions.name: Tantangara Creek
descriptions.description: Tantangara Creek in the open grassy country above the reservoir. Brumbies range through here, which is another reason to treat the water properly.

descriptions.name: Witzes Hut
descriptions.description: Old grazing hut on the plains near Tantangara, in open country with big skies and very little shelter. Camp outside and leave the hut for weather.

descriptions.name: Witzes Hut
descriptions.description: A second marker for the Witzes Hut site. Flat grassy ground around the hut; the nearest marked water is the creek back along the track.

descriptions.name: Bullocks Hill Trail
descriptions.description: Creek crossing on the Bullocks Hill Trail near Tantangara. Open grazing country with brumbies about, so treat the water, and expect it to be low in a dry summer.

descriptions.name: Tantangara Creek
descriptions.description: A second crossing of Tantangara Creek, lower in its valley. Larger here than up on the plain, but still seasonal and still to be treated.

descriptions.name: Murrumbidgee River
descriptions.description: The upper Murrumbidgee, one of the bigger river crossings on the trail. Depth varies with recent rain, and the water needs treating like everything else.

descriptions.name: Dairymans Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the grazing-era country north of the Murrumbidgee. A modest source that thins through summer; treat what you collect.

descriptions.name: Bally Creek 2
descriptions.description: Creek on the approach to Ghost Gully. Small and seasonal, and better checked on arrival than counted on from a distance. Treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Ghost Gully Camping Area
descriptions.description: Established camping area with vehicle access in the Long Plain country, which makes it a practical spot for a food drop or a lift out. Open ground and cold, clear nights.

descriptions.name: Boundary Creek
descriptions.description: The creek at Ghost Gully, the marked water for the camping area. Open grazing country upstream — treat it, and check the flow in a dry spell.

descriptions.name: Hainsworth Hut
descriptions.description: Hut on Dip Creek in the northern Kosciuszko country, another of the grazing-era shelters along this stretch. The creek beside it is the water; camp outside.

descriptions.name: Dip Creek 1
descriptions.description: Dip Creek at Hainsworth Hut. Small upland water that runs with the season; treat it before drinking.

descriptions.name: Dip Creek 2
descriptions.description: A second marked point on Dip Creek just past the hut. Same creek and the same caution — check it is running, and treat it.

descriptions.name: Morris Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the forested country between Dip Creek and the Bimberi approaches. Seasonal and best treated; carry enough not to depend on it.

descriptions.name: Seventeen Flat Creek
descriptions.description: Creek on the flats of the same name. Slow, grassy-banked water that suits filtering more than dipping a bottle; treat it whatever you do.

descriptions.name: Pocket Ck
descriptions.description: Small creek in the plains country before Oldfields Hut. A top-up rather than a plan, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Oldfields Hut
descriptions.description: Well-known grazing-era hut on the open plains below Bimberi, restored and much visited. Grassy camping around it, with the Goodradigbee close by for water.

descriptions.name: Goodradigbee River
descriptions.description: The Goodradigbee River in its upper valley near Oldfields Hut. Larger and more open than the ridge creeks; brumbies and stock have long used this country, so treat it.

descriptions.name: Dunns Flat Creek 1
descriptions.description: Creek on Dunns Flat, on the climb towards the Bimberi country. Small and seasonal — treat it, and top up before the higher ground.

descriptions.name: Dunns Flat Creek 2
descriptions.description: A second crossing of Dunns Flat Creek, higher in the catchment and correspondingly smaller. Treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Murray Gap Trail
descriptions.description: Marked water on the Murray Gap Trail, near the crossing into the ACT and the Bimberi Wilderness. High, small and seasonal; carry enough for the gap itself.

descriptions.name: Little Bimberi Creek
descriptions.description: Creek below Little Bimberi in the Bimberi Wilderness. Steep wooded country where the water is cold, small and seasonal — treat it.

descriptions.name: Bimberi Creek
descriptions.description: Bimberi Creek in the wilderness valley below the range. A better-sized creek than the ridge water above, though still seasonal; treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Cotter River
descriptions.description: The upper Cotter River in Namadgi, the catchment that supplies Canberra's water. A substantial stream by the standards of this section — treat it, and tread lightly in the catchment.

descriptions.name: Pond Creek 1
descriptions.description: Creek on the climb from the Cotter towards Cotter Gap. Small and seasonal; treat it, and fill here if it is running rather than banking on the gap.

descriptions.name: Pond Creek 2
descriptions.description: A second marked point on Pond Creek, up near Cotter Gap and the camping there. Higher in the catchment means less water — check it and treat it.

descriptions.name: Cotter Gap Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp at Cotter Gap in the Namadgi wilderness, a sheltered notch in otherwise steep country. Pond Creek nearby is the marked water for the site.

descriptions.name: Sawpit Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the Namadgi forest north of Cotter Gap. Seasonal like the rest of the water through here, so check it rather than assume it after a dry run of weeks, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Orroral River
descriptions.description: The Orroral River in its broad valley in Namadgi, lower and warmer country than the range behind. Treat the water, and expect the flow to drop away through summer.

descriptions.name: Honeysuckle Campground
descriptions.description: Formal campground at Honeysuckle Creek, on the site of the tracking station that carried the Apollo 11 moonwalk pictures. Vehicle access makes it an easy meeting or resupply point near the northern end.

descriptions.name: Booroomba Creek 1
descriptions.description: Creek below the Booroomba country in Namadgi, on the last stretch towards Tharwa. Small, seasonal, and to be treated.

descriptions.name: Booroomba Creek 2
descriptions.description: A second crossing of Booroomba Creek, lower down the valley. Handy for a last fill on the walk out; treat it.

descriptions.name: Georges Creek
descriptions.description: The last marked water on the trail, in low forest near the northern end in Namadgi, with under ten kilometres of walking left. Treat it like all the rest.

descriptions.name: Thomson Bridge Campground
descriptions.description: Vehicle-accessible campground by the Thomson River bridge, close to the southern end of the trail. The road access makes it a practical place to start, to finish a first day, or to leave a food drop.

descriptions.name: low saddle road 2
descriptions.description: A second marked water point on Low Saddle Road, away from the main line. Small ridge-country water: check it rather than count on it, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Nobs Track
descriptions.description: Another water point on Nobs Track, off the main line. Like everything at this height it runs with the season, so treat what you find and carry enough not to depend on it.

descriptions.name: Macalister Springs
descriptions.description: Spring below Mt Howitt and the classic water stop for this part of the trail. Being spring-fed it tends to hold on when surface creeks thin, but treat it, and still check it in a dry season.

descriptions.name: Vallejo Gantner Hut
descriptions.description: Distinctive memorial hut at Macalister Springs, one of the best-known huts in the Victorian Alps and a popular side trip. There is camping around it; the hut itself is shelter, not accommodation.

descriptions.name: Mt Murray Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp on the Mt Murray side trip in the Barry Mountains country. High, open ground with no water marked at the site, so carry up what you need for the night.

descriptions.name: Mt Hotham
descriptions.description: Alpine resort village on the Great Alpine Road, and the obvious resupply and exit point on the Victorian half of the trail. What is open changes a great deal with the season, so confirm services and transport before you plan a food drop around it.

descriptions.name: Spargo Hut
descriptions.description: Old hut in the high country near Mt Hotham, from the days when this was cattle and mining ground. Shelter for weather rather than a place to book a night; camp outside.

descriptions.name: Youngs Hut
descriptions.description: One of the old cattlemen's huts in the high country off the main line. Small and simple, and best thought of as shelter rather than a planned bed for the night.

descriptions.name: High Plains Creek
descriptions.description: Creek out on the Bogong High Plains away from the main line. Alpine water fed by snowmelt and bog, so it fades through summer; treat what you collect.

descriptions.name: Ryder's Huts
descriptions.description: Cattlemen's-era huts in the Bogong High Plains country, off the main line. Historic fabric worth leaving untouched; camp outside and use them only for shelter.

descriptions.name: Langford West Aqueduct 1
descriptions.description: The first marked point on the Langford West aqueduct, part of the old channel system that moves water across the high plains. There may or may not be water running in it, so look before you plan on it and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Falls Creek
descriptions.description: Alpine resort village at the edge of the Bogong High Plains, with sealed road access and the services of a small village. Much quieter outside the snow season, so check what is trading before relying on it for a resupply.

descriptions.name: Fitzgerald Hut
descriptions.description: Cattlemen's-era hut on the Bogong High Plains, reached on the side trip that also takes in Kelly Hut. Open, exposed country; the hut is shelter and camping is outside it.

descriptions.name: Kelly Hut
descriptions.description: The second of the pair of high plains huts on this side trip. Simple, historic and exposed — worth the look, and worth leaving exactly as you found it.

descriptions.name: Johnston Hut
descriptions.description: Small hut in the Bogong High Plains country off the main line. Old grazing-era fabric: use it for shelter, camp outside, and carry everything out with you.

descriptions.name: Big River
descriptions.description: Big River on the Mt Bogong alternate route, a separate crossing from the one on the main line. A real river, so crossings can be deep after rain, and the water needs treating.

descriptions.name: Bogong Creek Saddle
descriptions.description: Camp in the saddle above Big River, at the foot of the climb onto Mt Bogong on the alternate route. Exposed ground, and no water is marked at the saddle itself.

descriptions.name: Bogong Creek Saddle
descriptions.description: A second marked pitch at Bogong Creek Saddle on the Mt Bogong alternate. Fill down at the river before you settle in — this is the bottom of a long, steep climb.

descriptions.name: Cairn Creek Hut
descriptions.description: Small hut in the Big River country below Mt Bogong, away from the main line. Remote and simple, and a useful refuge if the weather catches you on the climb.

descriptions.name: Cleve Cole Hut
descriptions.description: Substantial stone memorial hut high on Mt Bogong, built after Cleve Cole died on the mountain in 1936 and still the main refuge up there. This is Victoria's highest country, where weather turns fast.

descriptions.name: Camp Creek
descriptions.description: The creek at Cleve Cole Hut on Mt Bogong, not to be confused with the Camp Creek at Mt Speculation on the main line. High alpine water: seasonal, and to be treated.

descriptions.name: Glen Wills wilderness retreat
descriptions.description: Accommodation at Glen Wills, an old goldfields locality on the road near Mt Wills and one of the few off-trail options on this stretch. Availability and access need arranging ahead.

descriptions.name: Omeo
descriptions.description: Town in the high country well away from the trail, reached by road rather than on foot, and the usual full-resupply option for the Victorian sections. Getting there means a lift or a shuttle, so arrange it ahead.

descriptions.name: Limestone Caves and Hut
descriptions.description: Hut in the limestone country around Limestone Creek, with the caves that give this side trip its name nearby. Caves need proper light and real care; the hut is shelter rather than accommodation.

descriptions.name: Bogong Creek Trib
descriptions.description: Small tributary in the Thredbo valley country away from the main line. A minor source that runs with the season, so treat it and don't build a plan around it.

descriptions.name: Thredbo
descriptions.description: Resort village in the Thredbo valley below the Main Range, and the main resupply and exit point on the New South Wales side. What is open and running varies with the season, so confirm before planning around it.

descriptions.name: Cootapatamba Hut
descriptions.description: Tiny emergency hut high on the Main Range near Lake Cootapatamba. It exists for people caught out by weather rather than for planned nights, and the ground around it is completely exposed.

descriptions.name: Snowy River 2
descriptions.description: A second marked point on the young Snowy River high in its catchment. Snowmelt-driven and strongest early in the season; treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Seamans Hut
descriptions.description: Stone memorial hut on the high slopes below Kosciuszko, built after skiers died in this country and kept as an emergency refuge ever since. Shelter only — camping is outside, and restricted up here.

descriptions.name: Wilkinson's Creek Campsite
descriptions.description: Camp beside Wilkinsons Creek in the high country below the Main Range. Alpine ground with camping restrictions in force, so check the park's current rules before choosing a pitch.

descriptions.name: Wilkinsons Creek
descriptions.description: Wilkinsons Creek, a snowmelt-fed alpine stream high in the Kosciuszko country. It runs hardest in spring and thins later in the season; treat what you collect.

descriptions.name: Opera House
descriptions.description: Small hut in the high Kosciuszko country with a memorable name and none of the grandeur to match it. Treat it as an emergency shelter, camp outside, and leave it clean.

descriptions.name: Horse Camp Hut
descriptions.description: Old hut in the Snowy Mountains off the main line, from the days when this was grazing and horse country. A refuge in weather rather than a place to plan a night around.

descriptions.name: Disappointment Ridge Hut
descriptions.description: Small hut on the high ground near Schlink Pass. Simple shelter in exposed country; camp outside, and keep it free for anyone who gets caught out.

descriptions.name: Munyang River
descriptions.description: Another marked point on the Munyang River, away from the main line. An upland river fed by the range above, with flows falling off through summer — treat it before drinking.

descriptions.name: Tin Hut
descriptions.description: Well-known hut in the Valentine and Schlink country of Kosciuszko National Park. Exposed, treeless ground all around; use the hut for shelter and camp outside.

descriptions.name: Mawsons Hut
descriptions.description: Hut in the Kosciuszko high country off the main line, one of the chain of old grazing-era shelters through this district. Camp outside and leave it as you found it.

descriptions.name: Derschkos Hut
descriptions.description: Small hut in the Jagungal country away from the main line. Another of the grazing-era shelters here — useful in weather, and not somewhere to plan a bed for the night.

descriptions.name: Brooks Hut
descriptions.description: Old hut in the northern Kosciuszko country off the main line. Simple shelter in open, cold ground; treat it as a refuge and camp outside it.

descriptions.name: Adaminaby
descriptions.description: Town out on the tablelands away from the trail, and a common road-access resupply and exit for the northern Kosciuszko sections. A working town rather than a resort, but you need transport to reach it.

descriptions.name: Happy Jacks Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the Happy Jacks country of northern Kosciuszko, away from the main line. Seasonal upland water — check it is running, and treat what you take.

descriptions.name: Happys Hut
descriptions.description: Hut in the Happy Jacks country, another of the old shelters scattered through northern Kosciuszko. The creek nearby is the water; camp outside the hut.

descriptions.name: Broken Dam Creek
descriptions.description: The creek at Broken Dam Hut, reached on a side trip. Small upland water that varies with the season, so treat it and look at it before relying on it.

descriptions.name: Broken Dam Hut
descriptions.description: Old hut in the northern Kosciuszko country, the point of this side trip. A simple grazing-era shelter with a creek nearby; camp outside and leave it as you found it.

descriptions.name: Four Mile Creek
descriptions.description: Creek at Four Mile Hut in the old Kiandra goldfields country — a different Four Mile from the one on the main line far to the south. Seasonal water, and it should be treated.

descriptions.name: Four Mile Hut
descriptions.description: Miner's hut from the Kiandra goldfields era, later caught up in this district's long skiing history. A well-loved little building: use it for shelter, camp outside, and leave it be.

descriptions.name: Long Plain Homestead
descriptions.description: Heritage grazing homestead out on Long Plain, in open, frost-prone country. Historic fabric worth respecting — camp outside rather than in the buildings.

descriptions.name: Yorkies Creek
descriptions.description: Creek on Long Plain away from the main line. Slow, open-country water in grazing and brumby country, so treat it properly, and expect less of it late in summer.

descriptions.name: Bally Creek 1
descriptions.description: The creek at Millers Hut, a separate marker from the Bally Creek point on the main line. Seasonal plains-country water — treat it, and check it rather than assume it.

descriptions.name: Millers Hut
descriptions.description: Small hut on the plains of northern Kosciuszko, reached on a side trip, with a creek alongside. Grazing-era shelter: use it for weather and camp outside.

descriptions.name: Old Currango Homestead
descriptions.description: Slab-built homestead on the Currango plains, said to be among the oldest surviving buildings in the park. Heritage fabric — look rather than lean, and camp well clear of the walls.

descriptions.name: Bill Jones Hut
descriptions.description: Small hut in the northern Kosciuszko plains country, the point of this side trip. Simple, historic and easily damaged; camp outside and leave it clean.

descriptions.name: Cave Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the limestone country of Cooleman Plain, where the water runs through gorge and cave systems. Karst water carries whatever is on the surface upstream, so treat it carefully.

descriptions.name: Magpie Flat Campground
descriptions.description: Camping area in the Blue Waterholes country on Cooleman Plain, with vehicle access. Open and popular ground; the creek nearby is the water, and it needs treating.

descriptions.name: Pockets Hut
descriptions.description: Hut in the northern Kosciuszko plains country, reached on a side trip. One of the old grazing shelters here — camp outside, and leave it for anyone caught out.

descriptions.name: Gurrangorambla Creek
descriptions.description: Creek in the northern Kosciuszko country away from the main line. Open grazing and brumby country upstream, so treat the water, and expect it to be low in a dry summer.

descriptions.name: Orroral Homestead
descriptions.description: Heritage homestead in the Orroral valley in Namadgi, near the site of the old space tracking station that gives this side trip its other half. Open grassy valley; look, but leave the buildings alone.
